stops.name: Denver Union Station
stops.teaser: A train station with a welcome arch that was torn down for being in the way.
stops.map: Denver Union Station, 1701 Wynkoop St, Denver, CO
stops.clue: Go to the LoDo neighborhood at 17th and Wynkoop Streets. Look for the stone station hall with a tall central tower and big orange letters.
stops.safety: Trains, buses and light rail all meet here. Stay on the platforms' public side, use crosswalks and watch for traffic on Wynkoop Street.

story: A station first opened on this spot on June 1, 1881, after four railroads agreed to share one "union" station. A fire in 1894 destroyed the middle of it, and a bigger one went up in the Romanesque Revival style.

On July 4, 1906, a huge arch was dedicated in front of the station. It cost $22,500, used 70 tons of steel and had more than 2,000 light bulbs. One side said "Welcome" and the other said "Mizpah", a farewell word. The arch was torn down in 1931 because it was considered a traffic hazard.

The current central building, in the Beaux-Arts style, opened in 1914. After a big renovation, the station house reopened in summer 2014 with the 112-room Crawford Hotel, shops and a modern open-air train hall.
stops.fact: The arch said "Welcome" on one side and "Mizpah" on the other.
stops.disputed: Many people call the whole building the 1881 station. Wikipedia says the central part was replaced after the 1894 fire and again in 1914.

claims.t: Denver's Mizpah Arch was dedicated in 1906.
The arch is still standing in front of the station.
claims.why: It was torn down in 1931 as a traffic hazard.

spot.why: One side said 'Welcome' and the other said 'Mizpah', a farewell word. The arch was torn down in 1931 because it was considered a traffic hazard.

stops.teaser: A triangle-shaped hotel where presidents slept and a football league was dreamed up.

story: The Brown Palace opened in 1892. Frank Edbrooke designed it in a triangle shape, and it was named for its owner, Henry C. Brown. When it was finished, it was the tallest building in Denver.
Wikipedia says an iron and steel frame covered in cement and sandstone made it one of America's first fireproof buildings. It is also one of the first atrium-style hotels ever built.

Theodore Roosevelt became the first sitting president to visit the hotel, on May 8, 1905. In 1959, Lamar Hunt and Bob Howsam met in the lobby to talk about a new football league, and Howsam agreed to own what became the Denver Broncos.
stops.fact: A plaque in the lobby marks the football meeting.
stops.disputed: Some stories say every president has stayed here. Wikipedia says nearly every one has visited, which is not the same thing.

claims.t: The hotel was the first in Denver, built before any other.

spot.why: When it was finished, it was the tallest building in Denver. Frank Edbrooke designed it in a triangle shape.

stops.name: Denver Mint
stops.teaser: The biggest coin factory in the world, behind a building copied from Florence.
stops.map: Denver Mint, 320 W Colfax Ave, Denver, CO
stops.clue: Go to Colfax Avenue near Cherokee Street in the Civic Center area. Look for the gray stone building that looks like an Italian palace.
stops.safety: Colfax Avenue is a busy road. Use crosswalks, view the building from the public sidewalk, and do not approach the secured areas.

story: Gold miners in the Colorado Gold Rush needed a place to turn gold dust into money. In 1860, a private firm, Clark, Gruber and Company, opened a mint at 16th and Market Streets that made gold coins.

The US government bought that building in 1863 and used it as an assay office. A new mint was planned in 1896, and construction on Colfax Avenue began in 1897. The first coins were struck on February 1, 1906.
The building is based on the Palazzo Medici-Riccardi in Florence, Italy. Today the Denver Mint is the single largest producer of coins in the world, with a D mint mark on its coins.
stops.fact: Coins from this mint carry a D.
stops.disputed: Many people think the mint has always sat on Colfax. Its first home was a two-story brick building at 16th and Market Streets.

claims.t: The Denver Mint struck its first coins in 1906.
claims.why: Wikipedia: first coins struck on February 1, 1906.

spot.why: The building is based on the Palazzo Medici-Riccardi in Florence, Italy. The first coins were struck there on February 1, 1906.

stops.name: Cheesman Memorial Pavilion
stops.teaser: A marble temple on a hill that used to be a cemetery.
stops.map: Cheesman Park Pavilion, E 8th Ave and N Humboldt St, Denver, CO
stops.clue: Go to Cheesman Park, southeast of downtown. On the east side, look for a white marble pavilion with a reflecting pool in front.
stops.safety: Stay on the paths, keep off the pavilion's steps if there is a fence or event, and watch for bikes and joggers.

story: The land that is now Cheesman Park was once a cemetery, opened in 1858. After years of neglect, Congress let the city turn it into a park in 1890. The park finally opened in 1907.
The park was named for Denver pioneer Walter Cheesman, whose family paid for the pavilion in his honor. The Cheesman Memorial was built in 1908 from Colorado Yule marble in the neoclassical style.

German-born landscape architect Reinhard Schuetze did the first designs, with winding carriage paths, the pavilion and a reflecting pool. From 1934 to 1972, the Denver Post sponsored open-air musicals and operas at the pavilion.
stops.disputed: Some visitors assume the pavilion is much older. Wikipedia says it was built in 1908, after the park opened.
